--------
In this VladTV interview, Chicago rapper Memo600 reflects on the aftermath of King Von’s fatal shooting in Atlanta on November 6, 2020, involving Quando Rondo’s camp and amid wider conversations around Lil Durk, NBA YoungBoy, O Block, and 600. Memo explains why he didn’t attend Von’s release party, saying he felt uneasy being the only 600 member around O Block that night.

After receiving frantic calls claiming both he and Von had been killed, Memo says he drove back to Chicago to clear his mind. The next day, while driving a new Range Rover with his baby mother and young cousin inside, the vehicle was shot at. Memo recalls rushing to the hospital after his cousin was struck and later died, describing the case as still unsolved. He also opens up about the grief, family fallout, and why he couldn’t bring himself to attend King Von’s funeral.

Poetik Flakko sits down with Vlad for a wide-ranging conversation about internet backlash, media rivalries, and the realities of building a career on YouTube. Flakko reflects on how Adam22 and No Jumper helped launch his platform, while explaining why the audience dynamic eventually became unhealthy. Vlad compares that criticism to years of being called “the police” in hip hop media, discussing DJ Akademiks, Charlamagne Tha God, Math Hoffa, Van Lathan, Big Boy, N.O.R.E., Elliott Wilson, and Peter Rosenberg.

The conversation turns to Corey Holcomb, the 5150 show, and Flakko’s issues with Holcomb after online comments and accusations. Vlad explains why he chose to speak with Corey privately, attend his stand-up shows, and move forward despite past tension. The interview also touches on Aries Spears, Ice-T, Black comedy audiences, No Jumper drama, media authenticity, and how public beefs play into the YouTube algorithm.

--------
Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev sits down with VladTV to discuss how the trading app helped reshape stock market access in the U.S., bringing an estimated 14 million first-time investors onto the platform. Tenev says Robinhood’s 28 million customers include a disproportionately large number of Black and Hispanic investors, challenging the old image of investing as mostly for wealthy older white men. The conversation covers Robinhood’s growth, a record quarter of roughly $1.3 billion in revenue, the impact of the GameStop era, and the company’s push toward 95% stock market participation.

Vlad also breaks down Vlad Stocks, portfolio-backed loans, margin rates, AMC, Robinhood stock, tokenization, taxes, and the future of Robinhood Social, where investors may share live portfolios and trades. A sharp discussion on retail investing, financial access, fintech, and how platforms like Robinhood are changing Wall Street.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/AxHbPY_r1q4
--------
Carlos Lehder sits down with Vlad to recount a pivotal 1981 encounter with Colombia’s M-19 guerrilla movement, describing how he escaped a kidnapping attempt after waking inside his own Jeep with his driver tied up. The former Medellín trafficking figure also addresses the abduction of Martha Nieves Ochoa and the violent response that followed, including the rise of MAS — “Death to Kidnappers.” Lehder disputes claims that he helped create the group, saying Pablo Escobar and Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha, “El Mexicano,” organized it, while he focused on personal security.

The conversation expands into the history behind the so-called Medellín Cartel, U.S. law enforcement labels, DEA attention, and how cocaine routes moved through Mexico, the Bahamas, Florida, and the United States. Lehder also discusses his Bahamas operations, alleged political protection, General Manuel Noriega’s role as mediator, and why he wrote his book to challenge long-running media narratives.

recentItems.description:

Part 1: https://youtu.be/s-3SalKgPTU
--------
In this Vlad interview, G. Dep recounts the night of October 19, 1993, when he was 18 years old and carrying a .40-caliber handgun during a failed robbery attempt that turned fatal. He explains how street image, drug culture and “idle time” influenced his choices before he approached 32-year-old John Henkel at 1 a.m. while riding a bicycle. G. Dep describes Henkel grabbing for the gun, the three shots that followed, and his decision to flee without taking any money. He also recalls throwing the weapon into the East River and going home uncertain whether Henkel had survived.

The conversation offers a stark look at fear, guilt and silence in an era before widespread cell phone video, surveillance cameras and modern policing tools, as G. Dep reflects on the choices that changed both his life and John Henkel’s forever.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/W6Vqal8IQfk
--------
William Noguera sits down with Vlad to break down the realities of San Quentin State Prison’s California death row in the 1980s, challenging common assumptions about rape, “punks,” and prison politics. Drawing on 40 years behind bars, Noguera explains how general population yards operated through strict affiliations, or “cars,” including Southern Mexicans, Northern Mexicans, the Mexican Mafia, Nuestra Familia, Bloods, Crips, BGF, and Border Brothers. He responds to Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza’s comments about high-ranking Mexican Mafia figures like Pegleg, insisting that during his time on death row, that behavior was not tolerated on GP yards. Noguera also details violent yard separations, protective custody, paperwork checks, informants, and the deadly stakes among condemned inmates, many convicted of multiple murders.
